Seminar Title:

ROLE OF EFFECTIVE DISCHARGE IN MEANDER INITIATION AND EVOLUTION

Abstract:

Meandering rivers are dynamic fluvial systems formed by complex interactions of flow hydraulics, sediment transport, and channel morphology. Effective discharge is identified as the flow condition that carries the highest proportion of sediment over a long-term period, and it is considered a dominant factor in channel adjustment of the governing hydrological variables. However, the role of effective discharge in initiating and controlling meander evolution is still not well understood, especially through an integrated approach that combines field observations, physics-based morphodynamic modeling, and artificial intelligence (AI). The main objective of this research is to develop an integrated framework to understand and predict the effect of effective discharge on the initiation and evolution of meanders in alluvial rivers. Initial estimates of effective discharge will be obtained using observed discharge and suspended sediment load data through conventional and entropy-based approaches, and its relation with sediment transport characteristics will be established. Then, a three-dimensional morphodynamic model will be developed using FLOW-3D HYDRO to study the effect of effective discharge on sediment transport, bed evolution, and meander development under different hydraulic and sediment conditions. A systematic sensitivity analysis will then be carried out to quantify the influence of hydraulic, sediment, and channel geometric parameters on meander evolution. Finally, field observations and numerical simulation outputs will be combined to develop AI-based predictive models to predict effective discharge and key morphodynamic responses. As a preliminary study to estimate effective discharge using an entropy-based approach, discharge and suspended sediment load data of two connected gauging stations in the Mahanadi River Basin have been analyzed. The preliminary results identified the dominant class of sediment-transporting discharge and demonstrated the applicability of the proposed methodology for effective discharge characterization. These results provide the hydrological basis for upcoming morphodynamic simulations with FLOW-3D HYDRO. The proposed research is expected to form a comprehensive framework linking effective discharge, sediment dynamics, and meander evolution. The results will improve the understanding of river morphodynamic processes and provide valuable insights for sustainable river management, restoration strategies, and hydraulic engineering applications.
